1.pericope_label: The priests the Levites shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel: the LORD is their inheritance

schools.summary: Calvin opens the chapter by laying out its structure and defending the tithe against the payer's resentment. The chapter contains three principal heads, of which the first shows that there was no reason why the Israelites should be aggrieved at paying tithes to the Levites, and at remitting the first-fruits and other oblations to the priests, since this tribe was deprived of their inheritance. God obviates all quarrels, and prevents unlawful gains and pilferings, by assigning their just share to the priests and Levites; and since God was as it were the lot of their inheritance, they justly claimed to themselves the right which he had transferred to them. If it were disagreeable to the people that their revenue should be tithed, God came as it were between, and declaring that it was his property in his right as King, appointed the Levites to be his stewards and collectors for receiving it — so that there was no ground for any one to raise a dispute, unless he chose professedly to rob God. Calvin observes that this declaration occurs often, since it was of great importance that the people should be assured God accounted as received by himself what he had assigned to the Levites, not only lest any portion should be withheld from them, but that every one should willingly pay the lawful dues of God's ministers, and lest any should wickedly murmur because the first-fruits and some portion of the sacrifices were appropriated for the subsistence of the priests. A second reason for paying the honour without grudging is also expressed: God had appointed them to be the ministers of his service, and the labourer is worthy of his hire. Gill limits the exclusion precisely — it is a having of no part in the land of Canaan, in the division of it among the tribes — and adds on the following verse that they were to have no inheritance among their brethren because provision was made for them otherwise.

Henry treats magistracy and ministry as two divine institutions of admirable use for the support and advancement of the kingdom of God among men, the laws of the former having been given in the close of the foregoing chapter and directions for the latter here; and he describes the passage as setting land-marks between the estates of the priests and those of the people. Care is taken, first, that the priests should not entangle themselves with the affairs of this life, nor enrich themselves with the wealth of this world, since they have better things to mind: they were to have no share either in the spoils taken in war or in the land that was to be divided by lot, their warfare and their husbandry being both spiritual, and enough to fill their hands with work and with profit and to content them. From this Henry draws his note — those that have God for their inheritance, according to the new covenant, should not be greedy of great things in the world, neither gripe what they have nor grasp at more, but look upon all present things with the indifference which becomes those that believe God to be all-sufficient. Care is likewise taken that they should not want any of the comforts and conveniences of this life; for though God, who is a Spirit, is their inheritance, it does not therefore follow that they must live upon the air. The people must provide for them, and must have their maintenance settled by law rather than left to depend upon the generosity of the people: he that is taught in the word ought in justice to communicate to him that teaches him, and he that has the benefit of solemn religious assemblies ought to contribute to the comfortable support of those that preside in such assemblies.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the passage as repetition rather than new legislation: with reference to the rights of the priests and Levites, Moses repeats verbatim from Numbers the essential part of the rule laid down there, and the expression 'all the tribe of Levi' includes the priests and Levites together. They were to eat the firings of Jehovah and his inheritance, as described in detail in the earlier law; and the inheritance of Jehovah consisted of the holy gifts as well as the sacrifices, that is, the tithes, firstlings and first-fruits. Moses felt it to be superfluous to enumerate these gifts one by one from the previous laws, and also to describe the mode of their application, or to define how much belonged to the priests and how much to the Levites — and Keil and Delitzsch add that however true it may be that the author assigns all these gifts to the Levites generally, the conclusion drawn from this by critics does not follow.

Clarke reports the rabbinic reading of the exclusion, that according to Maimonides it means they shall have no part in the spoils taken from an enemy, and glosses the positive side of the arrangement: the Lord being their inheritance means that he is the portion of their souls, and as to their bodies they shall live by the offerings of the Lord made by fire — the meat-offering, the sin-offering and the trespass-offering — since whatever was the Lord's right in these or other offerings he gave to the priests. Wesley identifies the phrase 'his inheritance' in the same way, as the Lord's portion or inheritance which God had reserved to himself, such as tithes and first-fruits and other oblations distinct from those which were made by fire.

3.pericope_label: This shall be the priest's due: the shoulder, the two cheeks, and the maw, and the firstfruit of thy corn

schools.summary: Clarke widens the scope of the due by way of the word for sacrifice, which is used to signify not only an animal sacrificed to the Lord but also one killed for common use; and in this latter sense he thinks it should probably be understood here, so that the command relates to what the people were to allow the priests and Levites from the animals slain for common use. He then specifies the three parts: the shoulder, probably cut off from the beast with the skin on, as Maimonides has it; the two cheeks, which may include the whole head; and the maw, meaning the whole of those intestines which are commonly used for food. On the first-fruits Clarke states the principle of the transfer briefly — all these first-fruits and firstlings were the Lord's portion, and these he gave to the priests. Wesley leaves the third item unsettled, noting that the Hebrew word rendered maw or stomach may have another signification, some rendering it the breast and others taking it for the part which lies under the breast.

Gill first fixes who owes the due: it comes not from the priests, as Jarchi observes, but from those that bring the sacrifices to the priests, and particularly the peace offerings. He identifies the first-fruits of corn, wine and oil as the terumah or heave offering, and notes that the measure or quantity is not declared in the law but was fixed by the Jews; and he reads the choosing as the choosing of the whole tribe of Levi out of all the other tribes of Israel. Calvin asks why the portions are enumerated at all, and answers that the list guards both sides. It is not only for the sake of the priests that God enumerates what he would have them receive, that they may obtain what is their own without murmuring or dispute; he also has regard to the people, lest the priests should basely and greedily take more than their due — which sacred history relates to have been done by the sons of Eli, who had advanced to such a degree of licentiousness that, like robbers, they seized violently on whatever their lust desired. Lest therefore they should give way to this gross covetousness, God prescribes to them certain limits, to which they were to confine themselves, so that if they transgressed them it was easy for any of the people to convict them of avarice.

Keil and Delitzsch render the law as the right of the priests on the part of the people, on the part of those who slaughter slain-offerings, whether ox or sheep, the offerer giving the priest the shoulder, the cheek and the stomach. They identify the parts technically: the first is the shoulder, that is the front leg, and the last is the rough stomach — the fourth stomach of ruminant animals, in which the digestion of the food is completed, the omasus or abomasus of the Latins, though the Vulgate has ventriculus here. On the choice of these three pieces in particular they report the observation of Münster and Fagius, that the animal possesses three principal parts, the head, the feet and the trunk, and that of each of these some portion was to be given to the priest who officiated. On the first-fruits they note that Moses is repeating the law already given in Numbers, and that he repeats it here for a particular purpose, to extend it to the first produce of the sheep-shearing. The ground of the whole right they take to be the choice of the tribe for the office of standing to minister in the name of Jehovah, for all the tribes — and to minister in the name of Jehovah means not merely by the appointment but also in the power of the Lord, as mediators of his grace. The words 'he and his sons', they add, point back quite to the Mosaic times, in which Aaron and his sons held the priest's office.

6.pericope_label: If a Levite come with all the desire of his mind unto the place which the LORD shall choose, he shall minister

schools.summary: Calvin treats this as the third head of the chapter and says it explains more clearly what is elsewhere more obscurely declared, since God had seemed to curtail from the Levites whatever he gave to the priests. He now more distinctly places the priests in the first rank, yet so that they should admit the Levites, on the score of their labours, to a share of the oblations. The sum of the law is that the Levites who remained at home should be content with the tithes and touch nothing of the other offerings, but that from wheresoever they should come to the sanctuary they were to be accounted as ministers and take their proper place. By this law it was provided that none should be excluded on the ground of the intermission of their duties, and that the condition of those who dwelt elsewhere should not be worse than of those who lived at Jerusalem; for although they might reside in other cities, they did not altogether cease from their ministry, since they had other duties to perform besides the sacrificing of the victims. Yet those who entirely devoted themselves to the work of the sanctuary were endowed by God with double honour, since it was by no means just that they should be defrauded of their maintenance who bade adieu to domestic cares and labours and occupied themselves totally in holy offices. Gill supplies the situation of the country Levites, who were dispersed all over the land and employed in instructing and teaching the people, and who, excepting the cities given them to dwell in out of the various tribes, were but sojourners; and on the portion he follows Jarchi, that they had equal parts of the sacrifices with the priests that usually ministered there, so that they divided the skins and flesh of the sin offerings, perhaps even such as did not come by virtue of the feast, as the daily sacrifices, the additions of the sabbath, the vows and the freewill offerings.

Wesley reads the qualifying phrase as marking a voluntary and permanent act: to come with all the desire of his mind is to come with full purpose to fix his abode and to spend his whole time and strength in the service of God. It seems, he says, that the several priests were to come from their cities to the temple by turns before David's time, and it is certain they did so after it; but if any of them were not contented with this attendance upon God in his tabernacle or temple, and desired more entirely and constantly to devote himself to God's service there, he was permitted so to do, because this was an eminent act of piety joined with self-denial, to part with those great conveniences which he enjoyed in the city of his possession. Wesley then quotes with approval a note written some sixty years before his own, which he thinks remarkable: a hearty, pious zeal to serve God and his church, though it may a little encroach upon a settled order, and though there may be somewhat in it that looks irregular, yet ought to be gratified and not discouraged — he that loves dearly to be employed in the service of the sanctuary, in God's name let him minister, and he shall be as welcome to God as the Levites whose course it was to minister, and should be so to them. On the reason for the equal portions Wesley is equally brief: he that waited on the altar ought to live by the altar, and it was fit that he should keep his money, wherewith he might redeem what he sold if afterwards he saw occasion for it. Clarke draws from the clause about the patrimony what it implies concerning Levitical property, that though the Levites might have no part of the land by lot, they were permitted to make purchases of houses, goods and cattle, and even of fields, as the cases of Abiathar and of Jeremiah show.

Keil and Delitzsch place this provision in line with what precedes: as the priests were to be remembered for their service on the part of the people, so the Levite also, who came from one of the towns of the land with all the desire of his soul to the place of the sanctuary, to minister there in the name of the Lord, was to eat a similar portion to all his Levitical brethren who stood there in service before the Lord. They correct a possible inference from the verb rendered 'sojourned', which does not presuppose that the Levites were houseless, but simply that they had no hereditary possession in the land as the other tribes had, and merely lived like sojourners among the Israelites in the towns which were given up to them by the other tribes. 'All his brethren the Levites' means the priests and those Levites who officiated at the sanctuary as assistants to the priests — from which, they note, it is assumed that only a part of the Levites were engaged at the sanctuary at any one time. Ellicott states the effect of the clause about the patrimony: the Levite thus dedicated was to have the same allowance from tithes as the rest who served at the tabernacle, beside the proceeds of the patrimony which he would have had in his own Levitical city.

9.pericope_label: When thou art come into the land, thou shalt not learn to do after the abominations of those nations

schools.summary: Calvin gives two accounts of the command, one of the danger it meets and one of the appetite behind the practices it forbids. It is too well known from experience how eagerly the human race lays hold of bad examples, and how prone it is to imitate them; and especially do those who come into a foreign land accustom themselves readily to its manners and customs. This is the reason why God expressly commands the Israelites to beware, lest, when they come into the land of Canaan, they should catch any infection from its inhabitants; the doctrine is universal in its application, but there was a necessity for providing against the danger which immediately impended. Calvin then finds in the verse a definition of the first commandment's breach: Moses explains clearly here what it is to have other gods, namely, to mix up the worship of God with things profane, since its purity is only maintained by banishing from it all uncongenial superstitions. The sum is that the people of God should abstain from all the inventions of men whereby pure and simple religion is adulterated. In general God wished to deter his worshippers from every fallacy whereby, from the beginning, Satan has deluded and fascinated miserable men, though he enumerates certain particular points which by usage and custom had obtained the greatest prevalence. To see what displeases God in these vices, Calvin looks at their root, and finds it good: men have a natural desire after knowledge, and even in the superstitious this has always proceeded from a good principle, inasmuch as God has implanted it in the minds of all when he would distinguish our race from the lower animals. Neither was there anything to be reprehended in this, that men, being conscious of their own ignorance, conceived that they were to obtain knowledge in no other way than by consulting God; that was the sole object of the Gentiles when they inquired of their magicians and sorcerers, to seek from heaven that knowledge of which they perceived themselves to be destitute — thus confessing that they were overwhelmed with darkness, and that the light of understanding was the special gift of God. Whence also came the name of divination, because they were persuaded that secret things were not within the compass of human apprehension, but that this knowledge must come from divine inspiration. The corruption enters because by his machinations the devil perverts what is right in itself. Gill hears in the opening clause the note of grace, since the land is so often described as what the Lord thy God giveth thee, to express the goodness of God in bestowing it as a mere favour of his without any desert of theirs, and so typical of the heavenly Canaan, or eternal life, which is the free gift of God through Christ.

Henry is astonished that the warning was necessary at all. One would not think there had been so much need as it seems there was to arm the people of Israel against the infection of the idolatrous customs of the Canaanites: was it possible that a people so blessed with divine institutions should ever admit the brutish and barbarous inventions of men and devils, and were they in any danger of making those their tutors and directors in religion whom God had made their captives and tributaries? It seems they were in danger, and therefore, after many similar cautions, they are here charged not to do after the abominations of those nations. Henry presses the same astonishment on his own age: one would wonder that such arts and works of darkness, so senseless and absurd, so impious and profane, could be found in a country where divine revelation shone so clearly, and yet we find remains of them even where Christ's holy religion is known and professed — such are the powers and policies of the rulers of the darkness of this world. He closes with a warning to his readers: let those that give heed to fortune-tellers, or go to wizards for the discovery of things secret, that use spells for the cure of diseases, or are in any league or acquaintance with familiar spirits, or form a confederacy with those that are, know that they can have no fellowship with God while thus they have fellowship with devils.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the shape of the catalogue that follows. Moses groups together all the words which the language contained for the different modes of exploring the future and discovering the will of God, for the purpose of forbidding every description of soothsaying; and he places the prohibition of Moloch-worship at the head of the list in order to show the inward connection between soothsaying and idolatry — possibly, they suggest, because the passing of children through the fire in the worship of Moloch was the more intimately connected with it.

10.pericope_label: There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son to pass through the fire, or useth divination

schools.summary: Clarke supplies the fullest philology in the chapter, taking the terms one at a time. The passing through the fire he thinks was probably a consecration to Moloch or some other deity, and holds that it is not likely their being burnt to death is here intended. Divination he explains as the practice of one who endeavours to find out futurity by auguries, using lots and the like; the observer of times is one who pretends to foretell future events by present occurrences, and who predicts great political or physical changes from the aspects of the planets, eclipses and the motion of the clouds; the enchanter he derives from a root meaning to view attentively, and identifies as one who inspected the entrails of beasts and observed the flight of birds and drew auguries from them, though some think divination by serpents is meant, which was common among the heathen; the witch is probably one who by means of drugs, herbs and perfumes pretended to bring certain celestial influences to her aid. The charmer he takes as one who uses spells — a peculiar conjunction, as the term implies, of words or of things, tying knots for the purposes of divination — and illustrates the custom from Virgil's shepherd knitting three knots of three colours and consecrating them to love. The consulter with familiar spirits is a Pythoness, one who inquires by means of one spirit in order to get oracular answers from another of a superior order; the wizard is a wise one or knowing one, the word having formerly been considered the masculine of witch, both practising divination by similar means; and the necromancer is one who seeks from or inquires of the dead, such as the witch at Endor, who professed to evoke the dead in order to get them to disclose the secrets of the spiritual world. Wesley reduces the same terms to their practical sense: divination is the foretelling of things secret or to come by unlawful arts; the observer of times superstitiously pronounces some days lucky and others unlucky, or divines by the motions of the clouds, by the stars, or by the flying and chattering of birds; the enchanter is a conjecturer who discovers hidden things by a superstitious use of words or ceremonies, or by observation of water or smoke or any contingencies; the witch is one that is in covenant with the devil; the wizard, in the Hebrew a knowing man, is one who by any forbidden ways undertakes the revelation of secret things; and the necromancer calls up and inquires of the dead.

Calvin allows both the milder and the extreme form of the Moloch rite. This horrible and altogether monstrous infatuation, whereby the Gentiles had been possessed, afterwards invaded the Jews also, so that they should immolate and even burn their children in honour of the gods to which they had devoted themselves; although it is probable that the greater part of them were not inflamed by such an excess of madness, but satisfied their superstition more easily by merely making their children pass through the fire, which was with them a kind of lustration to purge away all filthiness. Yet their cruel zeal impelled many of them even to murder, so as not even to spare their own flesh and blood — and in this they pleaded the example of Abraham, as if there were any similarity between the obedience of that holy man, who, led by God's command, was ready to slay his son Isaac, and this barbarous act of violence in people who, though God prohibited and gainsaid it, murdered their children. In this horrible spectacle, Calvin says, we perceive how much more fervently men engage in impious rites which their own temerity has dictated than in efforts to worship God aright, when he openly and expressly enjoins them the thing that is good. It ought indeed to be the first care of parents to consecrate their children to God; but the only rite of initiation for the Jews was circumcision, and with this they should have been content. On the arrangement of the list Calvin says he does not disapprove the view that Moses first uses a general term for all soothsayers and then proceeds to the particulars. Gill describes the Moloch rite as a sort of lustration by fire, two fires being made and the child led by a priest between them, which was an initiation of him into the religion of that deity and a devoting of him to it — Jarchi describing piles of fire made on this side and on that, with the children caused to pass between them both — and adds that besides this they used to burn them with fire to this deity, perhaps after the performance of the ceremony. Gill reports Aben Ezra and Ben Melech, who take divination for a general name whose particulars follow; and on the charmer he gives the rival accounts, one who pretends to cure diseases by charms or a charmer of serpents, or, according to Jarchi and the Targums, one who gathers serpents and scorpions and all kinds of creeping things into one place, while Aben Ezra makes him one who says certain words to gather demons together.

Keil and Delitzsch gloss the harder items of the catalogue, identifying the one who pronounced a ban as probably referring to the custom of binding or banning by magical knots, and the last two as the necromancer and the one who asked the dead, that is, who sought oracles from them. Ellicott adds the philological notes: the charmer is literally one who ties knots, a word used here for the first time in the Old Testament; the consulter with familiar spirits is literally one who consults ôb; the wizard is one who knows, or pretends to know, the secrets of the unseen world; and the necromancer is one who inquires of the dead. He also observes that in Hebrew the idea of 'time' in the second term is not so clear as the Rabbinical explanation makes it, and that the word seems rather to mean the practising of hidden arts. Ellicott closes with the judgment that separates him from the others in this chapter: four of these practices are ascribed to king Manasseh, and it is hardly possible that all of them were mere imposture and deceit.

12.pericope_label: All that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD: thou shalt be perfect with the LORD thy God

schools.summary: Gill narrows the reason clause with Jarchi: it is not that a man must do all these things, but whoever does any of them, and with them all those that consult such persons and make use of them; and it must be especially abominable in the people of Israel to encourage such persons and practices, who had the knowledge of the true God, and him to consult on all occasions, his law and testimony to attend unto as the rule of their conduct, and his prophets to advise with in matters of difficulty. He glosses the positive command as sincerely serving and worshipping God, faithfully adhering to his word, laws, statutes and ordinances, and walking uprightly before him. Calvin finds two restraints laid on Israel at once: God would have the authority of God act as a rein to guide them, and then sets before them that vengeance which they were soon about to see inflicted upon the heathen, nay, of which they were themselves to be the executioners and ministers. Since it could not be a matter of the slightest doubt that the inhabitants of the land of Canaan were rooted out from their peaceful habitations only by God's hand, he assigns as the cause of this destruction that they had polluted themselves and their country by these blasphemous and abominable superstitions; and by this striking example he deters them from imitating the sins which the facts themselves showed to be thus severely punished — as Paul admonishes believers to seek diligently to avoid the sins which provoke God's wrath against the disobedient. On the command to be perfect Calvin refers it to the mutual obligation of the holy covenant, whereby as on the one side God had pledged himself to the Jews, so on the other he had made them his debtors, not to prostitute themselves to idols or to hanker after strange religions, whereby men's minds are led astray. It is opposed to all those mixtures or corruptions which withdraw us from the sincere worship of the one true God, because the simplicity which retains us in obedience to heavenly teaching is that spiritual chastity which God requires in his Church; and the context proves it, since God would restrain the Jews from all licentiousness, so that being devoted to his service they should not look this way or that way, nor be carried away by vanity and instability, but constantly abide in the pure worship he had prescribed. For this reason Paul declares that he is jealous for Christ, and, having espoused the Corinthians to Christ, feared lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtlety, so being ensnared by the wiles of impostors they should fall from the simplicity that is in Christ. On the closing verse of the section Calvin adds that the inheritance was handed over on the condition that they should be mindful of so great a benefit and beware of all pollutions, and that they succeeded the former inhabitants with a view to their being separate from them; for whence was this change, except that God might acquire to himself a new people and purify the land from all its defilements? Though only two classes of superstition are named, they indicate them all — the sum being that they should not be like the nations in the vices and corruptions which had been the cause of their destruction, since God had exterminated not only the men themselves but their abominable rites also.

Keil and Delitzsch state the reason plainly — whoever did these things was an abomination to the Lord, and it was because of this abomination that he rooted out the Canaanites before Israel — and then mark the emphasis of the contrast that follows: Israel, on the other hand, was to be blameless with Jehovah, that is, in its intercourse with the Lord. The pronoun is placed first as a nominative absolute for the sake of emphasis, so that the sense is, but thou, so far as thou art concerned, not so; and though the heathen whom they exterminated before them hearkened to conjurers and soothsayers, Jehovah their God had not allowed anything of the kind to them. Ellicott renders the same clause more literally as, as for thee, not so hath Jehovah thy God given unto thee, and finds the contrast very marked between the miserable resources of idolatrous nations in their anxiety and the light and comfort promised to Israel, and to us, in the One Mediator — even Israel, he says, was better off than the heathen. He supports it from Rashi, who says on the words 'not so' that God has not left thee to hearken to observers of times and enchanters, for behold he has given the Shechinah to rest upon the prophets, and the Urim and Thummim. On the command to be perfect Ellicott preserves another note of Rashi's which he thinks worth having: thou shalt walk with him in sincerity, and wait for him, and thou shalt not pry into the future, but whatsoever cometh upon thee, take it with simplicity, and then thou shalt be with him and be his portion.

Wesley reads the command to be perfect as a demand for exclusive attachment — to be sincerely and wholly his, seeking him and cleaving to him and to his word alone, and therefore abhorring all commerce and conversation with devils. On the last verse of the section he supplies the forward reference which the chapter is about to take up: God has not suffered thee to follow these superstitious and diabolical practices, as he has suffered other nations to do, but has instructed thee better by his word and Spirit, and will more fully instruct thee by a great prophet.

15.pericope_label: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the promise stands at this point and then reaches a conclusion about its reference which sets him against every other witness in the chapter. It is added by anticipation, lest the Israelites should object that they were more hardly dealt with than the rest of the nations of the world; for it was always most justly considered an extraordinary blessing to hold communication with God, and indeed there can be nothing more to be desired. But an opinion had obtained currency that men approached more closely to God by means of magical arts, by the oracles of Pythonic spirits and by the study of augury, so that the people of Israel would have complained of being badly treated if they had been shut out from all prophecies and revelations. Moses meets this objection by announcing that their access to God would be not less familiar than as if he should himself openly come down from heaven, if only they kept the right way and were contented with that rule which he deemed best for them; he therefore commands that, instead of all the imaginations of the Gentiles, the doctrine of the prophets should alone have force among them, signifying that although God should not openly come down from heaven, yet his will, as far as was expedient, should be surely and clearly made known to them, since he would faithfully teach them by his servants the prophets. Calvin finds the same doctrine in Isaiah, who asks whether a people should not seek unto their God rather than unto them that have familiar spirits and wizards that peep and mutter, and who sends them to the law and to the testimony; and he has no doubt Isaiah took that doctrine from this passage, first condemning the errors which men by their curiosity invent for themselves and then enjoining the faithful simply to give attention to the Law. Hence he concludes that the word 'a Prophet' is used for a number of prophets. It is altogether absurd, as some do, to restrict it to Joshua or Jeremiah, since Moses is treating of the continual manner of the Church's government and is not speaking of what God would do within a short time; and not at all more correct, he adds, is the opinion of those who apply it strictly to Christ alone, since God's intention was that no excuse should be left for the Jews if they turned aside to familiar spirits or magicians. Gill takes the contrary view and rules out the alternatives one by one: not Joshua, as Aben Ezra, not Jeremiah, as Baal Haturim, nor David, as others, nor a succession of prophets, as Jarchi, for a single person only is spoken of, and there is a dissimilitude between Moses and any one of the prophets, and all of them in succession. It is the Messiah with whom the whole agrees, and upon this the expectation of a prophet among the Jews was raised. Gill fills out the prophetic office: he was a prophet mighty in word and deed, who not only foretold future events, such as his own sufferings and death and resurrection and the destruction of Jerusalem, but taught and instructed men in the knowledge of divine things and spake as never man did, preaching the Gospel fully and faithfully, so that as the law came by Moses, the doctrine of grace and truth came by him; and he was raised up of God, called, sent, commissioned and qualified by him for the office, as well as raised from the dead in confirmation of it.

Henry holds both readings of the promise together. Some think it is the promise of a succession of prophets that should for many ages be kept up in Israel: besides the priests and Levites, their ordinary ministers, whose office it was to teach Jacob God's law, they should have prophets, extraordinary ministers, to reprove them for their faults, remind them of their duty and foretell things to come, judgments for warning and deliverances for their comfort. Having these prophets, they need not use divinations nor consult with familiar spirits, for they might enquire of God's prophets even concerning their private affairs, as Saul did when he was in quest of his father's asses; nor could they miss the way of their duty through ignorance or mistake, nor differ in their opinions about it, having prophets among them whom in every difficult doubtful case they might advise with and appeal to. These prophets were like unto Moses in some respects, though far inferior to him. But whether a succession of prophets be included in this promise or not, Henry is sure that it is primarily intended as a promise of Christ, and calls it the clearest promise of him that is in all the law of Moses — expressly applied to our Lord Jesus as the Messiah promised by the apostles, echoed by the people when they said concerning him that this is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world, and confirmed by the fact that it was his Spirit that spoke in all the other prophets. Henry then states three things promised concerning Christ. There should come a prophet great above all the prophets, by whom God would make known himself and his will to the children of men more fully and clearly than ever he had done before: he is the light of the world, as prophecy was of the Jewish church, and the Word by whom God speaks to us. God would raise him up from the midst of them: in his birth he should be one of that nation, should live among them and be sent to them, and in his resurrection he should be raised up at Jerusalem, and thence his doctrine should go forth to all the world. And he should be like unto Moses, only as much above him as the other prophets came short of him — for Moses was such a prophet as was a law-giver to Israel and their deliverer out of Egypt, and so was Christ, who not only teaches but rules and saves.

Clarke sets the promise directly against what has just been forbidden: instead of diviners, observers of times and the rest, God here promises to give them an infallible guide, who should tell them all things that make for their peace, so that his declarations should completely answer the end of all the knowledge that was pretended to be gained by the persons already specified. Like unto Moses he takes to mean a prophet, a legislator, a king, a mediator, and the head or chief of the people of God — the very person of whom Moses was the type, and who should accomplish all the great purposes of the Divine Being; such a prophet as had never before appeared, and who should have no equal till the consummation of the world. This prophet, Clarke says, is the Lord Jesus, who was in the bosom of the Father and who came to declare him to mankind; every word spoken by him is a living infallible oracle from God himself, and must be received and obeyed as such, on pain of the eternal displeasure of the Almighty. Elsewhere in the chapter Clarke cites Ainsworth for the argument that Christ alone was like unto Moses as a prophet, since it is written that there arose not a prophet in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, so that the promise cannot be understood of the ordinary prophets which were raised up in Israel; that Christ was like Moses in his office of mediation between God and his people, but greater as being the mediator of a better covenant established upon better promises; and that as Moses excelled all the prophets in speaking to God mouth to mouth, so Christ excelled him and all men, in that being in the bosom of the Father he came down from heaven and declared God to us. Wesley reads 'will raise up' as meaning that God would produce and send him into the world in due time, and says that Christ was truly, and in all commendable parts, like Moses — in being both a prophet and a king and a priest and mediator, in the excellency of his ministry and work, in the glory of his miracles, and in his familiar and intimate converse with God.

16.pericope_label: According to all that thou desiredst in Horeb in the day of the assembly: and the LORD said unto me, They have well spoken

schools.summary: Calvin makes the whole passage turn on the usefulness of the terror the people felt at Sinai. He pronounces them guilty of ingratitude if they did not quietly submit themselves to their prophets, since on this point God had complied with their own request. For in order that the prophetic office might be more reverenced and beloved by them, and lest it should fall into disrepute through their beholding the prophet to be but a mortal, God had extracted the confession from them that nothing could be better than that he should make choice of human interpreters. At the promulgation of the Law the visible majesty of God had shone forth, and the people, terrified at the sight, had voluntarily desired that Moses should be given to them as a teacher and as the proclaimer of the heavenly voice; and Calvin has already remarked how useful this terror was to recommend the teaching which is delivered by the mouth of man. He presses the point on his readers: we have abundant experience that our minds are often carried away by vain speculations, so that we should wish to bring down God from heaven as often as any doubt creeps into them. It was necessary, therefore, that the Israelites should be convinced of their weakness, lest they should go beyond their due bounds; that they might be led to ask for that as a great blessing which God had foreseen to be for their good; and that they might at the same time abandon that proud curiosity which would always have been exciting them, had it not been corrected betimes by the application of this remedy. On the following verse Calvin is careful about what God's approval does and does not establish. Moses relates how this desire of the people was approved by the judgment and the voice of God — not as if whatever the foolish caprice of men may have urged them absurdly to ask ought therefore to be immediately granted, but that when God's consent and, so to speak, his vote coincides with it, then whatever he shows to be pleasing to him ought to stand firm and inviolable. Hence it follows that God, in sending the prophets, provided for the salvation of men as was most expedient; and Calvin adds that when pious teachers arise who faithfully show the way of salvation, it is an extraordinary proof of his favour, and he takes to himself the praise for it. Calvin's text preserves at this verse a note on the disputed reference, reporting that some of the Hebrews understand by that prophet Joshua, who succeeded Moses as ruler, while others think Jeremiah must be meant, who rebuked the people in the same terms as Moses had done; but that Christians who devoutly assert that this passage speaks of Christ confute the Jews by referring to what is said in the last chapter of Deuteronomy, that there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses — so that the passage must be prophetic of some other remarkable prophet who should not be inferior to Moses, and as Moses delivered the people from corporal bondage, so shall the prophet whom God will raise up for them deliver them from the bondage of sin. Gill supplies the occasion, that this was promised them in answer to their request at Horeb or Mount Sinai, when the law was delivered to them in the terrible manner it was, and that the day of the assembly was the day in which the tribes were gathered together at the foot of the mount to receive the law; and he notes that it was Moses who carried the request to the Lord.

Keil and Delitzsch draw the conclusion the wording invites: with this assurance the Lord had fully granted the request of the people, according to all that thou desiredst of the Lord thy God — and Israel therefore was all the more bound to hearken to the prophets whom God would raise up from the midst of itself, and not to resort to heathen soothsayers. They identify the phrase 'in the day of the assembly' with the same phrase used earlier in the book of the day at Horeb, and refer for the fact itself to the parallel accounts in Deuteronomy and Exodus.

18.pericope_label: I will put my words in his mouth; and whosoever will not hearken, I will require it of him

schools.summary: Gill observes that from the way the promise is introduced it seems to have been first made at Mount Sinai and is now renewed and repeated, though it is recorded nowhere else; and he draws out what it originally answered. The people were not only made easy for the present by the appointing of Moses to receive from the Lord all further notices of his mind and will, but were assured that when it was his pleasure to make a new revelation, or a further discovery of his mind and will, in future times, he would not do it in that terrible way in which he had delivered the law to them, but would raise up a person of their own flesh and blood by whom it should be delivered — which was sufficient to prevent their fears for the future. On the sanction Gill takes those who will not hearken to be those who slight and despise the doctrines of the Gospel, and the prophet who presumes to be one pretending a mission and commission from God who was never sent by him; and on the question that follows he observes that it is a thought arising in the mind, appearing to be a difficulty, upon which a query is made. Calvin pauses here to mark a division in the law itself. Thus far, he says, he has reviewed the supplements to the First Commandment which relate to the ancient types and to legal worship; the Commandment itself will always remain in force, even to the end of the world, and is given not only to the Jews but likewise to us also, but God formerly made use of the ceremonies as temporary aids, of which, although the use has ceased, the utility still remains, because from them it more clearly appears how God is to be duly served, and the spirit of religion shines forth in them. Now follow the political supplements, whereby God commands the punishments to be inflicted if his religion shall have been violated. Calvin defends the principle: political laws are not only enacted with reference to earthly affairs, in order that men should maintain mutual equity with each other and should follow and observe what is right, but that they should exercise themselves in the veneration of God. For Plato also begins from hence when he lays down the legitimate constitution of a republic, and calls the fear of God the preface of all laws; nor has any profane author ever existed who has not confessed that this is the principal part of a well-constituted state, that all with one consent should reverence and worship God. On the unspoken question Calvin explains why it had to be met. God, in his appointment of prophets to be his substitutes in teaching the people, had invested them with no common authority, enjoining obedience to be paid to their precepts; but those upon whom the office of teaching is conferred do not always duly fulfil it, and hence the doubt naturally arises how the people shall determine when they are addressed as by God's mouth, so as to distinguish the true from the false. There is therefore no question expressed in words, but God anticipates the secret scruples which might otherwise keep men's minds in suspense, for to say a thing in the heart is equivalent to doubting in oneself when any danger is perceived. To remove this difficulty God does not enumerate all the marks of distinction, because he does not allude to doctrine but only to prophecies; and, speaking popularly, as to evil and ignorant persons, he commands them to observe whether those who pretend to the name of prophet foretell the truth. Although, as Calvin has lately noted, false teachers also rival the servants of God in this respect and are found to be veracious in some particular prophecy, it is sufficient as the touchstone of their truth to set down what happens for the most part — just as God himself chooses to be distinguished and separated from idols by the same test.

Wesley glosses the sanction and then turns it into history: 'I will require it' means I will punish him severely for it, and the sad effect of this threatening the Jews have felt for above sixteen hundred years together.

22.pericope_label: When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, the LORD hath not spoken it

schools.summary: Gill states the test and then adds the qualification that keeps it from being mechanical. A prophet speaking in the name of the Lord says he comes from God, is sent by him, and has a commission from him to say so; if the thing follow not nor come to pass — as with the prophecy of Hananiah — that is the thing which the Lord has not spoken, or otherwise it would have come to pass, unless a condition is either expressed or implied, such as the repentance or the disobedience of a people. To speak presumptuously is to speak in a bold and daring manner, with great impiety and impudence, out of the prophet's own head and heart, the thing being a mere device and imagination of his own which, not having the fear of God, he delivered as coming from the Lord. On the closing clause Gill takes the command to cover both reproof and punishment: they were not to be afraid of such a prophet, not only to reprove him for his wickedness but also to punish him for it, showing no regard to the high character he assumes, nor to the great pretensions he makes to sanctity, knowledge and familiarity with God. Calvin distinguishes two faults in the presumption rather than one: God condemns not only the folly and vanity of those who advance their own inventions in the place of his commands, but also their arrogance, since this is impious and intolerable audacity, to set forth the offspring of man's earthly brain as if it were a divine revelation; and on this ground their impiety is detestable who fill the air with the fumes of their revelations in order to alarm the simple. He explains why the reassurance was needed at all: nothing can be more arrogant than the ministers of Satan, and they confidently utter their boastings, by which we may be easily moved and even overwhelmed, unless we had this buckler to protect us, namely that their terrific noise may be safely despised. Calvin then applies the doctrine to his own century without softening it. This doctrine, he says, is nowadays very useful for us: we know how insolently the Papists boast of the Catholic Church and of the Apostolic See, how fiercely they rage in Peter's name, and how impetuously they fulminate their curses and anathemas; but when it is ascertained that whatever they put forward as revelations of the Spirit are but the empty figments of men, it will be easy to dispel those terrors which flow from this same fountain of presumption.

Keil and Delitzsch state the criterion exactly: the false prophet was to be discovered by the fact that the word proclaimed by him did not follow or come to pass, that is, that his prophecy was not fulfilled, and of him they were not to be afraid — so that by this injunction the occurrence of what had been predicted is made the criterion of true prophecy, and not signs and wonders. Ellicott carries the same rule forward into the Gospel, calling it one form of our Lord's test for all prophets, that by their fruits — meaning the results of their teaching, and not its first impressions — ye shall know them.

Clarke notices a feature of the prophetic writings which makes the test workable: it is worthy of remark that the prophets in general predicted those things which were shortly to come to pass, that the people might have the fullest proof of their divine mission, and of the existence of God's providence in the administration of the affairs of men. Wesley states the test and its application in two strokes: the thing is what the prophet gives as a sign of the truth of his prophecy, and the falsehood of his prediction shows him to be a false prophet; to speak presumptuously is impudently to ascribe his own vain and lying fancies to the God of truth.
